system:
You are an assistant working with the Acme team. Its tracker project is ACME. Its code lives in acme/web and globex/api.
Prefer a tool over your knowledge for current state, and cite the repo, file or pull request.

Knowledge:
# llama-server configuration — copy to config/llama.yaml and edit.
#
# config/llama.yaml is gitignored, so this file is the record of the schema.
# Every value below is also validated by scripts/lib/common.sh; run
# `make test-unit` after changing the schema.

# Where to deploy. Auth comes from .env (SSH_KEY or SSH_PASS).
remote:
  host: 10.0.0.9
  user: youruser

runtime:
  engine: podman              # podman | docker — must match the target
  gpu: amd                    # amd | nvidia   — must match the target
  instances_dir: /opt/llm/instances
  router_map: /etc/llama-router/models.json

# Applied to every instance unless the instance overrides it.
defaults:
  # false = each slot gets its own dedicated window (predictable, more memory)
  # true  = one shared pool any single request may use (cheaper, slots contend)
  kv_unified: false

  # batch_size is logical, ubatch_size physical. ubatch <= batch.
  #
  # A large ubatch is only expensive when flash attention is OFF, because the KQ
  # tensor is then materialized and grows with n_ctx x n_ubatch. On this target
  # flash attention resolves to ON for every instance (see flash_attn below), so
  # that cost does not apply and ubatch_size: 2048 is what production runs.
  # UNMEASURED: no benchmark here compares ubatch values. If you change it,
  # record a `make benchmark` before/after rather than reasoning about it.
  batch_size: 2048
  ubatch_size: 2048

  # Convention here is threads_gen == physical core count (16 on this box, which
  # has 16c/32t), with batch/http lower. UNMEASURED: "hyperthreading hurts
  # inference" is widely repeated, is not tested anywhere in this repo, and a
  # previous tuning doc argued the exact opposite (deliberate oversubscription to
  # 20 threads). Nobody measured either position. Treat these as a working
  # default, not a finding — and if you change them, record a benchmark.
  threads_gen: 16
  threads_batch: 12
  threads_http: 6

  cache_reuse: 256            # prompt cache reuse threshold, lower = more aggressive

  # KV cache quantization. The two MUST match; validation rejects a mismatch.
  #
  # Memory is DERIVED and exact. KV bytes per token =
  #   2 x n_layers x n_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_value
  # For Qwen3-14B (40 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128), per 1024 tokens of `-c`:
  #   f16   160 MiB   (16.0 bits/value)
  #   q8_0   85 MiB   ( 8.5 bits/value — 53% of f16)
  #   q4_0   45 MiB   ( 4.5 bits/value — 28% of f16)
  #
  # Quality is MEASURED on this hardware — full method in specs/kv-quant-study.md,
  # produced by `make kv-study`. Same GGUF in every arm, KV type the only variable,
  # 131072 tokens per arm, over two corpora: prose (wikitext-2) and real
  # tool-calling turns rendered through the server's own chat template.
  #
  # Versus f16, on the tool-calling corpus:
  #   q8_0   mean KLD 0.0021   99.9% KLD 0.060   top-1 agreement 97.9%
  #   q4_0   mean KLD 0.0433   99.9% KLD 2.313   top-1 agreement 92.5%
  # So q4_0 costs ~20x the divergence of q8_0. q8_0 is the sane default; q4_0 is
  # a real quality trade, not a free memory win.
  #
  # Three numbers that used to live here are WITHDRAWN as unmeasured:
  #   "q8_0 = <0.1% quality loss" — the honest figure is 97.9% top-1 agreement,
  #     i.e. ~2% of tokens change their top choice. Small, not <0.1%.
  #   "q4_0 = ~50x the perplexity damage of q8_0" — measured at ~20x, not 50x.
  #   "asymmetric types fall back to CPU attention, 25-45x slower" — upstream
  #     attributes that figure to a CUDA build missing quantized-FA kernels, not to
  #     asymmetry. Asymmetric IS several times slower here (measured, on the GPU),
  #     which is one reason validation refuses it — but not 45x, and not via CPU.
  #
  # Also withdrawn: that q4_0 harms tool calling *specifically*. It does not —
  # top-1 agreement is 0.70pp BETTER on tool-calling content than on prose at q4_0.
  # What IS true is that the tail is amplified there (99.9% KLD 1.75x the prose
  # figure at q4_0, vs 1.27x at q8_0), and a malformed tool call is a tail event.
  cache_type_k: q8_0
  cache_type_v: q8_0

  # This knob does NOT turn flash attention off. false only omits -fa, which
  # leaves llama.cpp on its own default of `auto`.
  #
  # MEASURED on the target (journal, 2026-08-08, build b7966):
  #   llama_context: flash_attn = auto
  #   sched_reserve: Flash Attention was auto, set to enabled
  # So flash attention is ENABLED on all three instances despite this saying
  # false, and it runs on the GPU. An earlier version of this comment claimed
  # the AMD Vulkan backend has no FA kernel and falls back to CPU; that is not
  # what the target does, and the claim is withdrawn.
  #
  # A quantized cache_type_v REQUIRES flash attention — llama.cpp refuses to
  # start with "V cache quantization requires flash_attn" if it resolves to off —
  # so deploy warns when this says false alongside a quantized V cache.
  # Check the resolved value with `make status` (flash-at), never from this line.
  flash_attn: false

  # Speculative decoding. Needs a small draft model of the same family.
  # Empty string disables it. A quantized KV cache can collapse draft
  # acceptance, so prefer f16 when using this.
  draft_model: ""
  draft_max: 16

  container_image: docker.io/kyuz0/amd-strix-halo-toolboxes:vulkan-radv

# One entry per model. Each becomes llama-server@<name>.service reading
# <instances_dir>/<name>.conf, and each must already exist on the target —
# adding one also needs a router_map entry, which deploy does not manage.
#
# The instance NAME is what clients pass as "model".
instances:
  my-model:
    port: 8082
    model_file: Qwen3-14B-Q4_K_M.gguf

    # THE important number: what a SINGLE request gets.
    #
    # llama.cpp's -c is a TOTAL it divides across slots:
    #   n_ctx_seq = kv_unified ? n_ctx : PAD256(n_ctx / parallel_slots)
    # so setting -c directly is how you end up serving tiny windows by
    # accident. Deploy derives -c = context_per_request x parallel_slots and
    # refuses to proceed if the result wouldn't survive that rounding.
    #
    # Do not exceed the model's training context (40960 for Qwen3) — llama.cpp
    # caps the slot there and the extra KV is simply wasted.
    context_per_request: 16384

    # Concurrent requests for this model. Total KV scales with
    # parallel_slots x context_per_request.
    parallel_slots: 8

  # Instances inherit defaults and override only what differs.
  my-small-model:
    port: 8083
    model_file: Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf
    context_per_request: 4096
    parallel_slots: 8
    threads_gen: 8
    threads_batch: 6
    threads_http: 4

resources:
  limit_nofile: 65535
  limit_memlock: infinity

# There is deliberately no `benchmark:` block. Benchmark concurrency is derived
# from the instance's parallel_slots (scripts/benchmark.sh), so a second number
# here could only ever disagree with the server's real capacity — the previous
# one said 4 while the benchmark ran 8 VUs. Output length comes from
# BENCH_MAX_TOKENS. Nothing read this block.
# What KV cache quantization costs Qwen3-14B on this target

Generated by `scripts/kv-quant-study.sh` on 2026-08-09T04:58Z.
This file replaces asserted numbers with measured ones. Do not edit by hand;
re-run the script.

## Setup

| | |
|---|---|
| model | `Qwen3-14B-Q4_K_M.gguf` (identical across arms — only KV type varies) |
| context | `-c 8192`, `--chunks 16` = 131072 tokens per arm |
| flash attention | `--flash-attn on` explicitly, never `auto` |
| backend | Vulkan/RADV, gfx1151 |
| build | b7966-8872ad212 |

## Results

`base` is f16/f16 and is the reference every other arm is compared against,
so its KLD columns are empty by construction.

| corpus | arm | K | V | PPL | mean KLD | 99% KLD | 99.9% KLD | same top-1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| prose | `base` | f16 | f16 | 7.0837 | - | - | - | 100.000% |
| prose | `kv8` | q8_0 | q8_0 | 7.083076 | 0.001976 | 0.014515 | 0.046738 | 97.556% |
| prose | `kv4` | q4_0 | q4_0 | 7.233682 | 0.035879 | 0.338477 | 1.323230 | 91.806% |
| tools | `base` | f16 | f16 | 5.3728 | - | - | - | 100.000% |
| tools | `kv8` | q8_0 | q8_0 | 5.368609 | 0.002104 | 0.018035 | 0.059510 | 97.903% |
| tools | `kv4` | q4_0 | q4_0 | 5.482939 | 0.043287 | 0.497448 | 2.313263 | 92.509% |

## The differential — the actual question

"Does KV quantization hurt tool calling more than it hurts text?" is a ratio,
not an absolute. Below is each metric on `tools` divided by the same metric on
`prose`, per arm. **1.0 means no tool-calling-specific effect.**

| arm | mean KLD | 99% KLD | 99.9% KLD | same top-1 (pp difference) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `kv8` | 1.06x | 1.24x | 1.27x | +0.35 pp |
| `kv4` | 1.21x | 1.47x | 1.75x | +0.70 pp |

Read `same top-1` as the behavioural metric — it is the share of tokens where
the quantized cache still ranks the same token first. A **positive** pp difference
means the tool-calling corpus held up BETTER than prose.

## How to read this

- **same top-1** is the share of tokens where the quantized cache still ranks
  the same token first. This is the number that tracks behaviour.
- **99% / 99.9% KLD** are the tail. A mean KLD near zero with a fat tail means
  most tokens are fine and a few are badly wrong — which is exactly how a
  malformed tool call happens.
- **The differential is the finding.** Compare each arm's numbers on `tools`
  against the same arm on `prose`. Similar degradation means KV quantization
  is not specifically a tool-calling problem, whatever the folklore says.
- **`k4v8` is the diagnostic.** llama.cpp #23470 measured q4_0-on-K destroying
  Qwen2.5-7B (PPL ratio 196x, same top-1 98% -> 11.8%) while q4_0-on-V cost
  almost nothing. If `k4v8` collapses here and `k8v4` does not, K sensitivity
  is the whole story and `cache_type_k` is the only knob that matters.

## Raw logs

Kept on the target at `/opt/llm/kv-study/<corpus>.<arm>.log`.
The KLD reference files are ~18 GiB each; `--clean` removes them.
# Ollama backend (untested)

`scripts/install-ollama.sh` exists and is kept for reference, but **nothing in this
repo's test suite covers it**. None of `make deploy`, `make verify`, `make test-context`,
`make test-models`, or `make benchmark` works against an Ollama target — they all assume
llama.cpp semantics (`/props`, per-instance confs, `-c`/`-np` flags, the
`llama-server@<name>.service` template).

Treat anything below as unverified.

## What the install script does

```bash
sudo ./scripts/install-ollama.sh
```

Installs Ollama, configures systemd to bind `0.0.0.0:11434`, opens the firewall, and
optionally calls `scripts/setup-cloudflare.sh` to expose it through a tunnel.

## Why it isn't wired into the tooling

The context-window work this repo is built around does not transfer:

- Ollama sets context per-request (`options.num_ctx`) or per-Modelfile, not via a
  server-wide `-c` divided across slots. The `context_per_request` /
  `parallel_slots` derivation that `config/llama.yaml` encodes has no analogue.
- Concurrency is governed by `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` / `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS`,
  environment variables on the service, not per-instance config files.
- There is no `/props`, so `make verify`'s core assertion — that the *running* server
  reports the window we asked for — has nothing to read.
- Ollama loads and evicts models on demand with its own keep-alive timer, so the
  one-instance-per-model layout the deploy script manages doesn't apply.

## If you do want to use it

Point a client straight at `http://<host>:11434/v1/` — it speaks the OpenAI-compatible
API. Manage models with `ollama pull` / `ollama list` / `ollama ps` on the box.

To bring it under this repo's tooling properly, someone would need to:

1. Add an `ollama` runtime engine to `runtime.engine` validation in
   `scripts/lib/common.sh`.
2. Decide what `context_per_request` means for it — most likely a per-model Modelfile
   `PARAMETER num_ctx`, written and reloaded by deploy.
3. Give `verify-deploy.sh` something to assert against. `/api/show` returns model
   parameters and is the closest equivalent to `/props`.
4. Add fixtures and golden files so `make test-unit` covers the rendering, exactly as
   the llama.cpp path is covered today.

Until that exists, the honest position is that this backend is installable but unmanaged.

## Known interaction

Ollama and llama.cpp will contend for the same GPU if both run on one box — each keeps
its weights resident. On a machine already serving llama.cpp instances, starting Ollama
can push the total past VRAM and make whichever loads second fail to allocate.
# systemd template for one llama-server instance per model.
#
# THIS FILE IS THE ARGV. Everything llama-server is actually run with lives here,
# so a flag change is a reviewable diff instead of an undocumented edit on the
# target. Before this was vendored, 12 of the 17 variables deploy renders into
# <instances_dir>/<name>.conf had no consumer anywhere in the repo: you could add
# a knob to config/llama.yaml, deploy it, and have it reach nothing, with every
# offline test still green.
#
# TWO SUBSTITUTION LAYERS, DO NOT MIX THEM
#   at-sign placeholders -> replaced by scripts/deploy-llama.sh at render time
#                 from config/llama.yaml. Deploy refuses to install a unit with
#                 any left unresolved, so do not write one in prose here.
#   ${NAME}    -> left alone. systemd expands these per instance from
#                 EnvironmentFile, which is what deploy renders per model.
#   %i         -> left alone. systemd's instance name, i.e. the model name.
#
# The instance name is also the model name clients pass as "model", and nginx
# routes on it — see CLAUDE.md.
#
# Changing this file restarts EVERY instance, because they all share the
# template. `make deploy-dry` says so before you commit to it.
[Unit]
Description=LLaMA.cpp Inference Server (instance %i)
After=network.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
EnvironmentFile=@INSTANCES_DIR@/%i.conf

ExecStartPre=-@ENGINE_BIN@ rm -f llama-server-%i

# Wrapper because llama-server flags depend on FLASH_ATTN and DRAFT_MODEL which
# are conditional. systemd ExecStart can't do conditionals so we build the
# arg list in /bin/sh first and then exec the container engine.
#
# Note FLASH_ATTN=false does NOT pass -fa off, it passes nothing — which leaves
# llama.cpp on its own default of `auto`. Measured on this target, auto resolves
# to ENABLED. See the flash_attn comment in config/llama.example.yaml.
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c '\
    FA_ARG=""; \
    [ "$FLASH_ATTN" = "true" ] && FA_ARG="-fa"; \
    DRAFT_ARGS=""; \
    if [ -n "$DRAFT_MODEL" ] && [ "$DRAFT_MODEL" != "null" ]; then \
        DRAFT_ARGS="-md /models/$DRAFT_MODEL --draft-max $DRAFT_MAX -ngld 999"; \
    fi; \
    exec @ENGINE_BIN@ run \
        --name llama-server-%i \
        --rm \
@GPU_ARGS@
        -v @MODELS_DIR@:/models:ro \
        -p 127.0.0.1:${LLAMA_PORT}:${LLAMA_PORT} \
        -e LLAMA_API_KEY=${LLAMA_API_KEY} \
        ${CONTAINER_IMAGE} \
        @SERVER_CMD@ \
            --alias %i \
            --no-mmap \
            -ngl 999 $FA_ARG \
            -c ${CONTEXT_SIZE} \
            -np ${PARALLEL_SLOTS} \
            -b ${BATCH_SIZE} \
            -ub ${UBATCH_SIZE} \
            --cont-batching \
            --cache-prompt \
            --cache-reuse ${CACHE_REUSE} \
            -t ${THREADS_GEN} \
            -tb ${THREADS_BATCH} \
            --threads-http ${THREADS_HTTP} \
            --cache-type-k ${CACHE_TYPE_K} \
            --cache-type-v ${CACHE_TYPE_V} $DRAFT_ARGS \
            -m /models/${MODEL_FILE} \
            --host 0.0.0.0 \
            --port ${LLAMA_PORT} \
            --metrics'
            # NOTE: inside the container llama-server binds 0.0.0.0:${LLAMA_PORT}.
            # Host security comes from -p 127.0.0.1:${LLAMA_PORT}:${LLAMA_PORT}
            # which restricts the host-side bind to loopback. nginx (also on
            # host loopback) is the only thing that can reach these ports.
            #
            # --metrics is required by `make status`. --jinja is deliberately NOT
            # passed: llama-server has defaulted jinja on since build b7170
            # (PR #17524), and `make verify` proves streamed tool calls work by
            # making one rather than by looking for a flag. If you ever pin a
            # container image older than b7170, add --jinja here.

ExecStop=@ENGINE_BIN@ stop llama-server-%i

Restart=always
RestartSec=10
# Model load from cold page cache can take minutes; a short timeout here shows up
# as a deploy that "failed" while the server was still starting normally.
TimeoutStartSec=600

LimitNOFILE=@LIMIT_NOFILE@
LimitMEMLOCK=@LIMIT_MEMLOCK@

StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=llama-server-%i

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)
